objectives: Explain what market failure and externalities are, and tell examples of negative and positive externalities apart.
Distinguish and calculate private cost, external cost, and social cost (and private, external, and social benefit).
Use a graph and equations to explain why, when there is an externality, the market quantity ends up above or below the socially optimal quantity.

concepts.definition: A situation in which the outcome the market produces on its own differs from the allocation of resources that is best for society as a whole. Externalities, public goods, and common resources are the classic causes.
A cost or benefit that a transaction or activity imposes on a third party who is not part of it, without any payment changing hands.

An externality that imposes uncompensated harm on third parties, such as pollution, noise, or congestion. Because producers do not count that harm as a cost, the market produces more than the socially optimal quantity.

An externality that gives third parties a benefit they do not pay for, such as vaccination or spillovers from research and development. The good ends up produced and consumed below the socially optimal quantity.
Private cost is the cost that producers or consumers pay themselves. Social cost is the cost to society as a whole: private cost plus the external cost borne by third parties.
Private benefit is the gain received by the people in the transaction. Social benefit is private benefit plus the external benefit received by third parties.
The quantity that is best once all social benefits and social costs are counted. With a negative externality the market quantity is larger than this; with a positive externality it is smaller.

beginner.summary: When a deal harms or helps people who were not part of it, that is called an externality. When that happens, the market makes too much or too little.

sections.heading: Markets don't always get it right
paragraphs: In the last course, you learned that markets use prices to match how much people want to buy with how much people want to sell. But sometimes the result a market reaches on its own is not good for society as a whole. This is called market failure. Market failure does not mean markets are useless. It means there are certain situations where markets miss something, and you need to know what they are before you can fix them.

sections.heading: What happens to people outside the deal
paragraphs: When a factory makes and sells a product, the factory and its customers both get what they want. But what if smoke from the factory chimney makes people in the neighborhood cough? Those neighbors were not part of the deal, yet they were harmed. Harm or benefit that falls on people outside a deal is called an externality.

If it causes harm, it is a negative externality. Car exhaust and late-night construction noise are examples. If it creates a benefit, it is a positive externality. When you get a flu shot, you are less likely to get sick, and so is the friend sitting next to you, because you are less likely to pass the flu on.

sections.heading: The cost you pay and the cost everyone pays
paragraphs: The only costs the factory counts are its private costs, like materials, electricity, and wages. The neighbors' doctor bills caused by the smoke never show up in the factory's books. Add that harm to the private cost and you get the social cost. In the same way, the benefit of a flu shot to you is a private benefit; add the benefit your friends get and you have the social benefit.

sections.heading: So the market makes too much or too little
paragraphs: Because the factory does not pay for the harm, production feels cheaper than it really is, so the factory makes more than is best for society. With flu shots, you are not paid for the benefit your friends get, so fewer people get vaccinated than is best for society. When there is an externality, the market can easily miss the right amount.

intermediate.summary: An externality drives a wedge between private cost (or benefit) and social cost (or benefit). The size of that gap determines how far the market quantity strays from the social optimum.

sections.heading: What market failure means
paragraphs: A competitive market reaches equilibrium where the benefits and costs that buyers and sellers themselves consider are equal. If those benefits and costs capture every benefit and cost to society, the market equilibrium is also socially desirable. But if someone's benefit or cost is left out, the market equilibrium no longer matches the social optimum. That mismatch is market failure.

sections.heading: Externalities run in two directions
paragraphs: An externality is a cost or benefit that falls, without payment, on a third party who is not part of the transaction. Pollution, noise, and traffic congestion are negative externalities; vaccination, education, and spillovers from research and development are positive externalities. The key point is that these effects are not reflected in the price: whoever causes harm does not pay for it, and whoever creates a benefit is not paid for it.

sections.heading: Private cost, external cost, and social cost
paragraphs: Social cost = private cost + external cost, and social benefit = private benefit + external benefit. The supply curve reflects producers' private costs, so with a negative externality the curve representing social cost lies above the supply curve by the amount of the external cost. The demand curve reflects consumers' private benefits, so with a positive externality the curve representing social benefit lies above the demand curve by the amount of the external benefit.

sections.heading: Overproduction and underproduction
paragraphs: Negative externality: the socially optimal quantity is where the demand curve meets the social-cost curve, but the market trades where demand meets the (private) supply curve, so it trades more than the optimum (overproduction). Positive externality: the optimum is where the social-benefit curve meets the supply curve, but the market trades less than that (underproduction). On the graph, the vertical distance between the two curves is the external cost (or benefit) per unit.

advanced.summary: If the external cost per unit is constant, the social-cost curve is the supply curve shifted straight up by that amount. Solving for both equilibria as a system of equations measures the size of the overproduction.

sections.heading: Market failure as an efficiency benchmark
paragraphs: The social optimum is the quantity at which the social marginal benefit of the last unit equals its social marginal cost. The market stops where private marginal benefit (the demand curve) equals private marginal cost (the supply curve). When these two conditions differ, changing the quantity could raise society's total net benefit. That is the precise meaning of market failure.

sections.heading: Writing externalities as equations
paragraphs: Supply Qs = c + dP means that at price P, producers keep producing until private marginal cost reaches P. If the external cost per unit is a constant md, social marginal cost equals private marginal cost + md, so the social-cost curve is Qs = c + d(P − md). In other words, it is the supply curve shifted up vertically by md.
A positive externality attaches to the demand side instead. If the external benefit per unit is mb, the social-benefit curve is Qd = a − b(P − mb), that is, the demand curve shifted up by mb.

sections.heading: How large is the overproduction?
paragraphs: With demand Qd = a − bP, supply Qs = c + dP, and external cost per unit md, the market quantity is Q_m = a − b(a − c)/(b + d) and the socially optimal quantity is Q* = a − b(a − c + d·md)/(b + d). The difference is Q_m − Q* = b·d·md/(b + d), which is larger when the external cost is larger and when demand and supply are more sensitive to price.

For every unit overproduced, social marginal cost exceeds social marginal benefit, so the losses on those units add up to the social loss caused by the externality. Lesson 3 shows how a tax can shrink this gap.

worked_examples.title: The social cost of a paper mill
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: A paper mill spends $300 on materials, electricity, and labor to make 1 ton of paper. Wastewater from the mill means a town downstream has to spend $100 per ton of paper to clean its water. What is the social cost of 1 ton of paper, and how much of that cost does the mill not feel?
worked_examples.answer: The social cost is $400 per ton, and the external cost the mill does not feel is $400 − $300 = $100.

worked_examples.title: The positive externality of vaccination
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: A flu shot costs $35. The student who gets it receives a benefit worth $30 (private benefit), and the people around the student benefit by $10 because their risk of infection falls (external benefit). Will the student get the shot? Is the shot worthwhile for society as a whole?
steps: The student's comparison: private benefit $30 < cost $35, so on their own the student skips the shot.
Social net benefit = $40 − $35 = $5, so the shot is worthwhile for society as a whole.
worked_examples.answer: Deciding alone, the student does not get vaccinated, but society gains $5, so vaccination is desirable. When this happens across many people, fewer get vaccinated than the social optimum (underconsumption).

worked_examples.title: Measuring overproduction
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: In a market, demand is Qd = 90 − P and supply is Qs = 2P, and every unit produced creates an external cost of $6. Find the market equilibrium and the social optimum, and calculate the amount of overproduction.
steps: Market equilibrium: 90 − P = 2P, so P = $30 and Q = 60.
Social optimum: 90 − P = −12 + 2P, so P = $34 and Q = 56.
Overproduction = 60 − 56 = 4 (the same as the formula b·d·md/(b + d) = 1 × 2 × 6 / 3 = 4).
worked_examples.answer: The market trades at P = $30 and Q = 60, but the social optimum is P = $34 and Q = 56. The market produces 4 units too many.

graphs.title: Private cost and social cost
graphs.caption: Hypothetical example (worked example 3). Supply curve S reflects private cost; S′ adds the $6 external cost to show social cost. The market quantity is Q = 60; the socially optimal quantity is Q = 56.

real_world_examples.title: Why pollution leads to overproduction
paragraphs: A firm that releases pollutants does not pay for the harm suffered by the people around it. Because social cost is greater than private cost, the market produces more of the product than is socially desirable, and more pollution results.

real_world_examples.title: Spillovers from vaccination and research
paragraphs: Vaccination lowers the risk of infection not only for the person vaccinated but also for the people nearby. New technology and knowledge are used not only by the firm that developed them but also by other firms and by society. With positive externalities like these, the market supplies less than the socially desirable amount, so governments sometimes fill the gap with subsidies or research funding.

sdg_case.title: Exhaust and noise outside the school: where should we start?
paragraphs: SDG 13 calls for urgent action to combat climate change, and SDG 7 aims for affordable, clean energy for everyone. Cars that burn fossil fuels create negative externalities in the form of greenhouse gases and exhaust fumes.

Hypothetical situation: Drop-off and pick-up traffic crowds the road in front of a school, causing heavy exhaust and noise. Drivers weigh only their own time and fuel costs, not the harm to students. The city and the school want to choose a way to reduce this externality.

options.name: Restrict cars in front of the school during drop-off and pick-up
costs: Families who need to drive their children face real inconvenience.
Traffic may shift onto nearby streets.
assumptions: The rule can be enforced, and the harm does not simply move to other streets.

options.name: Raise parking fees around the school
benefits: People who really need to drive still can, while those with less need cut back first.
Fee revenue can be spent on safe routes to school.
costs: Lower-income families may feel the burden more heavily.
It is hard to know in advance how much driving will fall.
assumptions: Higher fees actually lead drivers to use their cars less.

options.name: Add school buses and bike lanes
benefits: The benefits of clean transportation grow.
Greenhouse gas emissions fall over the long run.
costs: It requires a budget and construction time.
If few people use them, the effect is small.
assumptions: Students and families actually switch to the new options.

discussion: The three options correspond to setting the quantity directly, changing the price, and adding alternatives. Considering both the size of the externality and fairness, which combination would work best?

key_takeaways: An externality is a cost or benefit that falls, without payment, on a third party outside a transaction, and it is a leading cause of market failure.
Social cost = private cost + external cost; social benefit = private benefit + external benefit.

A negative externality leads to overproduction, and a positive externality leads to underproduction. If the external cost per unit is constant, the social-cost curve is the supply curve shifted up by that amount.
